items.title: SELFIX: An Interactive System for Natural Self-Voice Approximation
items.authors: Pavo Orepic(University of Zurich); Steven Moran(University of Zurich; University of Neuchâtel); Volker Dellwo(University of Zurich; )
items.abstract: Most of us feel discomfort when we hear our recorded voice. This is because our voice is filtered by head vibrations during natural speech. Characterizing this filter may therefore recreate natural self-voice. Previous attempts relied on spectral equalization and failed to converge on a universal filter, likely due to unguided search across vast acoustic spaces. We introduce SELFIX, an interactive system that constrains this search with perceptually motivated dimensions, such as pitch and vocal-tract control. In a preliminary study (N = 25), participants repeatedly adjusted four randomized, unlabeled sliders. Consistent adjustments with high match and confidence ratings support SELFIX's validity. While all participants boosted low frequencies, males also lowered pitch and increased vocal-tract length, indicating that self-voice approximation extends beyond mere spectral equalization. These findings establish a structured acoustic basis for scalable, personalized self-voice modeling.

items.title: Noise Scaling Factor for the One-Dimensional Voice Production Model
items.authors: Tsukasa Yoshinaga(University of Osaka); Takeshi Ikuma(Louisiana State University); Brad H. Story(University of Arizona)
items.abstract: Sounds generated by turbulence at the glottis, such as those observed in breathy voice, affect voice quality. Although aerodynamic noise originating in the vocal tract has been incorporated in one-dimensional (1D) acoustic models, the accuracy of these models has rarely been examined. In this study, we evaluated the scaling factor used in a 1D noise model for vowel /a/ and /u/ by comparing with results from three-dimensional (3D) flow simulations that explicitly computes sound generation from turbulent airflow. Results showed that, for normal phonation in the vowel /a/, the conventional scaling factor yielded good agreement with the 3D results. In contrast, in breathy phonation where the glottis did not fully close, and in configurations with supraglottal constrictions of vowel /u/, the optimal scaling factor changed from the conventional value. These findings suggest that turbulence noise modeling in 1D approaches needs to be adjusted to the flow configuration of the vocal tract.

items.title: Improved modeling of vocal fold contacting and de-contacting in a geometric vocal fold model
items.authors: Tianyi Zhang(TU Dresden); Zihao Huang(TU Dresden); Peter Birkholz(Dresden University of Technology, Germany)
items.abstract: This paper presents a geometric model of the vocal folds for more natural-sounding articulatory speech synthesis. In contrast to similar models, we propose a biomechanically-motivated more gradual opening and closing of the glottis during the phases of partial contact of the vocal folds. This was combined with a mechanism to skew the glottal area waveform to the left or right. The model was implemented in the articulatory speech synthesizer and compared against a similar model without the improved contacting and de-contacting mechanisms in a perception experiment with synthetic sentences for a range of pre-phonatory model settings. In an A/B comparison, the synthetic sentences with the new model were preferred over the same sentences with the previous model in 58.1 % of the comparisons. In addition, the mean opinion scores for the quality on a five-point scale were 3.02 and 2.68 for the new and previous models, respectively.

items.title: The Effect of Neck Skin Vibration on the Periauricular Acoustic Receiver
items.authors: Ruoyan Li(Huawei); Yuhao Sun(Huawei); Fan Fan(Huawei)
items.abstract: During self-voicing, vocal cord vibrations propagate through the vocal tract and surrounding tissues, generating air-borne acoustic components radiated from the oral cavity as well as structural vibrations in the neck and its surface. This study investigates the impact of neck skin vibrations on periauricular acoustic receivers during self-voicing. The recordings were acquired under self-speech conditions using an array of microphones positioned at various locations on the head. Comparative analyses were conducted using experiments with a dummy head, real human speech tests and simulations. The results showed that periauricular acoustic receivers located near the neck detected significant air-borne acoustic components associated with neck skin vibrations. This finding holds significant implications for refining self-speech simulation models that treat mouth radiation as the sole acoustic source.

items.title: Investigating Human-Model Discrepancies in Speech Quality Assessment via Acoustic and Prosodic Perturbations
items.authors: Masato Takagi(Nagoya Institute of Technology); Masaya Kawamura(LY Corporation); Reo Shimizu(LY Corporation); Yuma Shirahata(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: Mean opinion score (MOS) prediction models are widely used as proxy metrics in text-to-speech (TTS) research, yet their ability to capture quality differences beyond acoustic fidelity remains unclear. We investigate this via controlled perturbations on speech: acoustic degradation, prosodic errors, and manipulation of speaker-specific characteristics such as pitch and speaking rate. We obtained MOS predictions for these speech samples from both human listeners and the model, and analyzed the differences in their perceptual characteristics. Results show that most models track acoustic degradation well, while all are insensitive to prosodic errors despite large subjective score drops. For speaker characteristics, models exhibit a double dissociation: strong mean fundamental frequency (F0) biases absent in human ratings, yet insensitivity to speaking rate and F0 variability that humans notice. These findings highlight limitations of scalar MOS prediction beyond acoustic fidelity.

items.title: Do speech foundation models perceive speaker similarity as humans do?
items.authors: Minoru Kishi(Keio University); Hayato Yagi(Keio University); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University; The University of Tokyo); Yuki Saito(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: This study presents a comparative analysis between the speaker embeddings of speech foundation models and human subjective perception of speaker similarity. Human listeners have the ability to judge speaker similarity on a continuous scale discerning how similar two voices are. In contrast, speech foundation models embed speaker characteristics into numerical representation. However, a question remains: does the numerical distance between speaker embeddings in these models truly align with the similarity perceived by humans? To address this, we conduct a comprehensive investigation using more than 40 models to compare model-derived distances with human-perceived similarity scores. Furthermore, we identify which factors in model configuration contribute most to a speaker embedding that mirrors human perception. Our findings provide insights for the development of more perceptually grounded speech foundation models.

items.title: What Makes Us Hate Our Own Voice? Large-scale experiments on Playback–Imagery Gaps and Individual--Speech Feature Effects
items.authors: Koki Fukuda(Keio University); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University; The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: This study examines factors associated with the playback-imagery gap underlying voice confrontation. Listening to one's recorded voice (playback) can be uncomfortable and has been attributed to a mismatch between expected self-voice (imagery) and the recording, yet the factors associated with this gap remain unclear. With Japanese participants (N = 459), we compared impression ratings after playback of one's recorded utterances versus imagery of producing the same utterances using counterbalanced block order. Playback produced more negative affective evaluations than imagery, especially higher discomfort, whereas self-likeness did not show the same pattern. Exploratory trait-acoustic interactions suggested listener-specific weighting of acoustic cues in self-voice evaluation. The gap also varied with order and block structure, suggesting contextual modulation. These results provide evidence relevant to self-voice aversion and motivate listener-adaptive models and more controlled follow-up studies for self-voice applications.

items.title: SGAD: A State-Guided Adaptive Decision Framework for Robust EEG-Based Auditory Attention Switch Decoding
items.authors: Yuting Ding(Southern University of Science and Technology); Xuefei Wang(Southern University of Science and Technology); Ximin Chen(Southern University of Science and Technology); Chunlin Li(Capital Medical University); Fei Chen(Southern University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Achieving robust EEG-based auditory attention switch decoding (AASD) is crucial for intelligent hearing aids. However, its application is limited as EEG non-stationarity complicates sequential decision-making, and insufficient control of potential confounding factors may overestimate performance. Therefore, we propose a state-guided adaptive decision (SGAD) framework that infers attention transition states via causal state detection and dynamically modulates temporal smoothing through state-guided adaptive gating. We further introduce six hierarchical evaluation protocols to assess generalization across audio, speaker, and subject dimensions. Experimental results show that SGAD improves decoding accuracy and stability while maintaining low response latency across evaluation scenarios. Performance variations across protocols further suggest data partition-related biases. Together, these findings advance robust AASD for neuro-steered hearing applications.

items.title: LipAdapter: Text-to-Video Alignment is All You Need for Lip-to-Speech
items.authors: Souvik Ghosh(IIIT Hyderabad); C. V. Jawahar(IIIT Hyderabad); Vinay Namboodiri(University of Bath)
items.abstract: Lip-to-Speech synthesis aims to generate intelligible, natural-sounding, and temporally synchronized speech from silent visual recordings of a speaker. Although recent end-to-end models have shown promising results, they require large amounts of training data and often lack out-of-dataset generalization. In this work, we introduce LipAdapter, a generic and efficient modular framework that adapts an existing frozen pre-trained Text-to-Speech model into a lip-synchronized speech generator. LipAdapter bridges the modularity gap between frozen Visual Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech models by aligning phoneme representation and lip embeddings via a novel text-to-video alignment module. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks in English while using 15× less training data than previous methods. We also demonstrate the model's zero-shot capabilities in multilingual lip-to-speech synthesis in French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. Code and demo are available at: https://lipadapter.github.io/.

items.title: How Bilingual Are SSL Speech Models? Cross-Lingual Probing of Articulatory Encoding with Finnish and Russian EMA
items.authors: Ailín Pollio San Pedro(University Grenoble Alpes); Tomi Kinnunen(University of Eastern Finland); Alexandre Nikolaev(University of Eastern Finland); Ruchi Pandey(University of Eastern Finland)
items.abstract: SSL speech models capture rich phonetic, prosodic, and acoustic patterns from raw audio, yet how they encode articulatory information across diverse languages remains unclear. Using EMA data from bilingual Finnish–Russian speakers, we evaluate cross-lingual correlations between SSL latent representations and articulatory movements. Models achieve strong prediction performance (Pearson r up to 0.68) even with ~5 minutes of training data, with multilingual models outperforming monolingual ones. Intermediate layers encode articulatory features most effectively, and tongue movements are more predictable than lip movements. We also assess the impact of task type (read versus spontaneous speech) and language proficiency, finding higher accuracy for structured tasks and strong generalization across proficiency levels. These results enhance the interpretability of SSL models and show their potential for speech-technology applications.
